questions.stem: An ellipse is written as $\dfrac{x^{2}}{25}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{9}=1$. Its major axis measures
questions.solution:
In $\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ the larger denominator sits under the variable that runs along the long axis. Here $25>9$, so the long axis is horizontal and
$$a^{2}=25,\qquad a=5.$$

The letter $a$ is only the **semi**-major axis — half of the full axis. The axis itself runs from $(-5,0)$ to $(5,0)$, so its length is
$$2a=10.$$
distractorRationale: Used the small denominator: $2b=2\times 3=6$ is the minor axis, not the major one.
Correct. $a^{2}=25$ gives $a=5$, and the major axis is $2a=10$.
Stopped at the semi-major axis $a=5$, forgetting the factor $2$.
Read off $b=3$, the semi-minor axis, which is the shortest of the four quantities on offer.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The ellipse
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — the three lengths.** $a^{2}=100$ and $b^{2}=64$, so $a=10$ and $b=8$. For an ellipse the focal half-distance comes from
$$c^{2}=a^{2}-b^{2}=100-64=36,\qquad c=6.$$

**Step 2 — the ratio.** Eccentricity is the focal half-distance divided by the semi-major axis:
$$e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac{6}{10}=\frac{3}{5}.$$

A value below $1$ is the sanity check: every ellipse has $0<e<1$.
distractorRationale: Correct. $c=\sqrt{100-64}=6$ and $a=10$, so $e=\dfrac{6}{10}=\dfrac{3}{5}$.
Used $\dfrac{b}{a}=\dfrac{8}{10}$. That ratio measures how round the ellipse is, but eccentricity needs $c$, not $b$.
Inverted the ratio to $\dfrac{a}{c}=\dfrac{10}{6}$. Any answer above $1$ cannot be an ellipse's eccentricity.
Computed $\dfrac{a-b}{a}=\dfrac{10-8}{10}$, subtracting the lengths instead of subtracting their squares.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The ellipse
questions.stem: An ellipse centred at the origin has foci $(\pm 4,\ 0)$ and semi-minor axis $3$. Its equation is
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — where the long axis points.** Both foci sit on the $x$-axis, so the major axis is horizontal and the equation has the form $\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ with $a>b$.

**Step 2 — the missing length.** The foci give $c=4$, and the semi-minor axis gives $b=3$. For an ellipse the relation runs
$$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}=9+16=25.$$

**Step 3 — assemble.**
$$\frac{x^{2}}{25}+\frac{y^{2}}{9}=1.$$
Check it: $(5,0)$ and $(0,3)$ both satisfy it, and $c=\sqrt{25-9}=4$ puts the foci back where they started.
distractorRationale: Put the larger denominator under $y^{2}$, which pushes the foci onto the $y$-axis instead of the $x$-axis.
Took $a^{2}=c^{2}=16$, treating the focus as the vertex. The focus always lies strictly inside the ellipse, so $a>c$.
Correct. $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}=9+16=25$, with the major axis horizontal because the foci are.
Used $b^{2}=c^{2}=16$, confusing the semi-minor axis with the focal half-distance.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The ellipse
questions.stem: $P$ lies on $\dfrac{x^{2}}{25}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{16}=1$, whose foci are $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$. The perimeter of $\triangle PF_{1}F_{2}$ is
questions.solution:
The perimeter is $|PF_{1}|+|PF_{2}|+|F_{1}F_{2}|$, and each piece is fixed even though $P$ is not.

**Step 1 — the two focal radii.** The defining property of an ellipse is that the two distances to the foci always add to $2a$. Here $a=5$, so
$$|PF_{1}|+|PF_{2}|=10.$$

**Step 2 — the base.** $c^{2}=25-16=9$, so $c=3$ and the foci are $(\pm 3,0)$. They are $2c=6$ apart.

**Step 3 — add.**
$$10+6=16.$$
The answer does not depend on which point $P$ is, which is what makes the question quick.
distractorRationale: This is $2a$ alone — the two focal radii — with the side $F_{1}F_{2}$ never added.
Added only $c=3$ instead of the full focal separation $2c=6$.
Used $2b=8$ for the base, taking the semi-minor axis where the focal half-distance $c$ was needed.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The hyperbola
questions.stem: $\dfrac{x^{2}}{36}-\dfrac{y^{2}}{13}=1$ meets the $x$-axis at two vertices. How far apart are they?
questions.solution:
Set $y=0$ to find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis:
$$\frac{x^{2}}{36}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\pm 6.$$

The vertices are $(-6,0)$ and $(6,0)$, so the gap between them is
$$6-(-6)=12.$$

That gap is the transverse axis, $2a$, with $a=6$.
distractorRationale: Gave $a=6$, the distance from the centre to one vertex, rather than the distance between the two vertices.
Took $2b$ from the $y$-term. That is the conjugate axis, and a hyperbola never actually reaches it.
Correct. $y=0$ gives $x=\pm 6$, so the vertices are $2a=12$ apart.
Doubled $a$ twice, reporting $4a$ instead of $2a$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The hyperbola
questions.stem: Asymptotes of $\dfrac{x^{2}}{9}-\dfrac{y^{2}}{16}=1$ have slopes $\pm k$, with $k>0$. Find $k$.
questions.solution:
Replace the $1$ on the right by $0$ — that is what the curve tends to far from the centre:
$$\frac{x^{2}}{9}-\frac{y^{2}}{16}=0.$$

This factorises into two straight lines. Rearranging,
$$y^{2}=\frac{16}{9}x^{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=\pm\frac{4}{3}x.$$

So $k=\dfrac{4}{3}$: take the square roots first, and the $y$-denominator goes on top.
distractorRationale: Used $\dfrac{a}{b}$. The slope of an asymptote is rise over run, so the number from the $y$-term belongs on top.
Correct. Setting the right-hand side to $0$ gives $y=\pm\dfrac{4}{3}x$.
Skipped the square roots and reported $\dfrac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}$.
Skipped the square roots and inverted the ratio as well.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The hyperbola
questions.stem: A hyperbola has foci on the $x$-axis, with $a=3$ and $b=4$. Its eccentricity is
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — find $c$.** A hyperbola adds where an ellipse subtracts:
$$c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}=9+16=25,\qquad c=5.$$

**Step 2 — divide.**
$$e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac{5}{3}.$$

Sanity check: every hyperbola has $e>1$, and $\dfrac{5}{3}>1$.
distractorRationale: Divided $c$ by $b$. Eccentricity always compares $c$ with $a$, the distance to a vertex.
Reported $\dfrac{b}{a}$, which is the asymptote slope, not the eccentricity.
Inverted the ratio to $\dfrac{a}{c}$. A hyperbola cannot have $e<1$.
Correct. $c=\sqrt{9+16}=5$, so $e=\dfrac{5}{3}$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The hyperbola
questions.stem: A hyperbola centred at the origin has a vertex at $(3,\ 0)$ and a focus at $(5,\ 0)$. Its equation is
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — orientation.** The vertex and the focus both sit on the $x$-axis, so the branches open left and right and the $x^{2}$ term carries the plus sign.

**Step 2 — the two given lengths.** The vertex gives $a=3$ and the focus gives $c=5$.

**Step 3 — the third length.** For a hyperbola,
$$b^{2}=c^{2}-a^{2}=25-9=16.$$

So the equation is
$$\frac{x^{2}}{9}-\frac{y^{2}}{16}=1.$$
Substituting $(3,0)$ returns $1$, as it must.
distractorRationale: Correct. $a^{2}=9$ from the vertex and $b^{2}=c^{2}-a^{2}=16$ from the focus.
Swapped the two denominators, which moves the vertex to $(4,0)$ instead of $(3,0)$.
Used $b^{2}=c^{2}=25$, forgetting to subtract $a^{2}$.
Gave the minus sign to $x^{2}$, which turns the branches upwards and puts the vertices on the $y$-axis.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The parabola
questions.solution:
Match the curve to the standard form $y^{2}=4fx$, whose focus is $(f,0)$ and whose directrix is $x=-f$.

Comparing coefficients,
$$4f=12 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f=3.$$

So the focus is $(3,0)$, three units to the right of the vertex, and the directrix is the line $x=-3$.
distractorRationale: Gave the directrix $x=-3$. The focus and the directrix sit on opposite sides of the vertex, so the sign flips.
Correct. $4f=12$ gives $f=3$.
Halved the coefficient instead of quartering it. $6$ is the focus-to-directrix distance, not the focal abscissa.
Read the coefficient itself as the coordinate, skipping the comparison with $y^{2}=4fx$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The parabola
questions.stem: A point on $y^{2}=8x$ sits $6$ units from the focus. Its $x$-coordinate is
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — locate the directrix.** Writing $y^{2}=4fx$ with $4f=8$ gives $f=2$, so the directrix is $x=-2$.

**Step 2 — use the focal distance rule.** Every point of a parabola is as far from the focus as from the directrix. For a point with abscissa $x$, the horizontal gap to the line $x=-2$ is $x+2$, so
$$x+2=6.$$

**Step 3 — solve.**
$$x=4.$$
distractorRationale: Correct. The focal distance is $x+2$, and $x+2=6$ gives $x=4$.
Used an offset of $4$ instead of $2$, halving the coefficient $8$ rather than quartering it.
Took the distance itself as the abscissa, ignoring the shift caused by the directrix.
Added the offset instead of subtracting it, solving $x-2=6$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The parabola
questions.stem: A chord $AB$ of $y^{2}=4x$ passes through the focus. If the two endpoints satisfy $x_{A}+x_{B}=6$, then $|AB|$ is
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — the directrix.** From $4f=4$ we get $f=1$, so the directrix is $x=-1$.

**Step 2 — turn each focal radius into a horizontal distance.** A point of the parabola is as far from the focus as from the directrix, so
$$|AF|=x_{A}+1,\qquad |BF|=x_{B}+1.$$

**Step 3 — add.** Because the chord runs through $F$, its length is the sum of the two radii:
$$|AB|=(x_{A}+1)+(x_{B}+1)=x_{A}+x_{B}+2=6+2=8.$$

How steeply the chord runs never enters this count.
distractorRationale: Reported the sum of the abscissae, leaving out the two shifts to the directrix.
Added one shift instead of two — only one endpoint was converted into a focal radius.
Correct. $|AB|=x_{A}+x_{B}+2=8$.
Used a shift of $2$ per endpoint, taking the focus-to-directrix distance rather than $f=1$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Conic Sections / The parabola
questions.stem: On $y^{2}=2px$ with $p>0$ and focus $F$, a point $M(x_{0},\ y_{0})$ satisfies $|MF|=2x_{0}$. Then $x_{0}$ equals
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — read the standard form.** Comparing $y^{2}=2px$ with $y^{2}=4fx$ gives $f=\dfrac{p}{2}$, so the directrix is $x=-\dfrac{p}{2}$.

**Step 2 — write the focal distance.** The distance from $M$ to the directrix is the horizontal gap, so
$$|MF|=x_{0}+\frac{p}{2}.$$

**Step 3 — impose the condition.**
$$x_{0}+\frac{p}{2}=2x_{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{p}{2}=x_{0}.$$

So $x_{0}=\dfrac{p}{2}$, which is positive, as any point on the right-opening branch must be.
distractorRationale: Used a directrix offset of $\dfrac{p}{4}$, quartering $p$ as though the equation read $y^{2}=4px$.
Took the offset as $p$ itself and solved $x_{0}+p=2x_{0}$, skipping the halving in $f=\dfrac{p}{2}$.
Doubled the previous slip, solving $x_{0}+2p=2x_{0}$.
Correct. $|MF|=x_{0}+\dfrac{p}{2}=2x_{0}$ leaves $x_{0}=\dfrac{p}{2}$.
